specStatements.text: The amount of energy stored in or released from a system as its temperature changes can be calculated using the equation:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
change in thermal energy, ∆ E, in joules, J
specific heat capacity, c, in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C
temperature change, ∆ θ, in degrees Celsius, °C
The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.

Required practical activity 1: investigat ion to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials. The investigation will involve linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to the increase in temperature and subsequent increase in thermal energy stored.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 5.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 5.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only AT 1 and AT 5 are drawn on, and only as far as this practical needs them: using apparatus to make and record accurate measurements of mass, temperature and time (AT 1), and safe use of apparatus to measure an energy transfer (AT 5). No other apparatus-and-technique skill is claimed for this practical, and no particular apparatus is presented as compulsory beyond what those two skills require. The statement is an index of skills rather than examinable content, so it carries no questions of its own.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Working scientifically and mathematical skills appear only where they genuinely arise in this practical: insulating the block and controlling other variables, evaluating the effect of energy transferred to the surroundings, converting grams to kilograms, and making one quantity the subject of ∆E = m c ∆θ. The full WS and MS descriptors are not reproduced or paraphrased, because the specification places them in 'Key opportunities for skills development' rather than in this section, so this statement carries no questions of its own.

scopeNotes.statement: Required practical activity 1: investigat ion to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials. The investigation will involve linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to the increase in temperature and subsequent increase in thermal energy stored.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The equation and the practical are applied only to a system whose temperature changes. Energy transferred during a change of state, and specific latent heat, are not used here; the specification places them in the particle model content, not in 4.1.1.3. Because the specification prescribes no single method, the electrically heated metal block is treated as one example of linking the decrease of an energy store to a temperature rise, not as the required method.

concepts.definition: The object, or group of objects, whose energy is being considered. In this section the system is the material whose temperature changes — for example a metal block, or the water in a beaker.
The energy stored in, or released from, a system as its temperature changes, measured in joules, J. It is a change, not a total: it does not say how much energy the system stores altogether.

concepts.term: Word equation for a temperature change
concepts.definition: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change. All three factors multiply, so leaving one out, or dividing by one of them, makes the answer wrong by that whole factor.
The symbol form of the same equation: ∆E is the change in thermal energy, m the mass, c the specific heat capacity and ∆θ the temperature change. The symbol ∆ always means 'change in'.
The mass of the material whose temperature changes, in kilograms, kg. A mass given in grams must be divided by 1000 before it is used, because the unit of c already contains 'per kilogram'.

The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius. It is a property of the substance, so every sample of that substance has the same value whatever its mass.

The unit of specific heat capacity: joules per kilogram per degree Celsius. The unit is a direct reading of the definition — joules of energy, for each kilogram, for each degree Celsius of temperature rise.
The difference between the final and the starting temperature, in degrees Celsius, °C. It is found by subtraction before the equation is used, and it is never the final temperature on its own.

An investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials by linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to the rise in temperature and so to the increase in thermal energy stored. Measuring the energy supplied, the mass and the temperature rise gives c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).

Energy that leaves the heated block or liquid and warms the room instead. It makes the measured temperature rise smaller than the supplied energy alone would produce, so uninsulated apparatus gives a value of c that is too high.

concepts.term: Accurate measurement in this practical (AT 1 and AT 5)
concepts.definition: The apparatus and technique skills this practical draws on: recording mass, temperature and time accurately (AT 1), and safely using apparatus such as an immersion heater and joulemeter to measure an energy transfer (AT 5).

concepts.term: Handling the equation and its units (WS and MS)
concepts.definition: The mathematical and working-scientifically demands that arise here: converting grams to kilograms, making c the subject of ∆E = m c ∆θ, and evaluating how energy transferred to the surroundings affects the result.

misconceptions.question: Water is heated from 18 °C to 78 °C. What value of ∆θ goes into ∆E = m c ∆θ?
misconceptions.misconception: ∆θ is the temperature the substance ends up at, so 78 is the number to substitute.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The final temperature is what the thermometer actually shows at the end, so it feels like 'the' temperature of the experiment. The ∆ symbol is easily read as decoration rather than as an instruction to subtract.
misconceptions.correction: ∆ always means 'change in'. Do the subtraction first and write that number down before touching the equation. Check it against a case where nothing happens: water left at 18 °C stores no extra energy, and only the subtraction gives ∆θ = 0.

misconceptions.question: Does a 2 kg block of copper have twice the specific heat capacity of a 1 kg block of copper?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both have the same specific heat capacity, because c is a property of the substance, not of the sample.
misconceptions.misconception: A bigger lump of a substance has a bigger specific heat capacity, because it takes more energy to heat it up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The bigger block really does need more energy for the same temperature rise, so students attach that fact to c instead of to m. The word 'specific' is not everyday language, and its technical meaning — 'per kilogram' — is easy to skip over.
misconceptions.correction: The mass is already accounted for separately, by m in the equation. 'Specific' means the quantity has been divided by mass, so c is fixed for a given substance; doubling the mass doubles ∆E through m and leaves c untouched.

misconceptions.question: A 300 g sample of water is heated. What number is used for m?
misconceptions.correct: 0.300 kg. The mass must be converted from grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass can be put straight into the equation in grams, because grams are a unit of mass too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balances in the laboratory read in grams, and students are used to the number they measured being the number they use. The 'per kilogram' hidden inside J/kg °C is not visible in the symbol equation itself.
misconceptions.correction: The unit of c fixes the unit of m: because c is joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, m must be in kilograms. Convert first, then sanity-check the size of the answer — 300 g of water cannot need millions of joules for a modest temperature rise.

misconceptions.question: Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C and aluminium has 900 J/kg °C. For the same mass and the same energy supplied, which warms up faster?
misconceptions.correct: The aluminium. A high specific heat capacity means more energy is needed for each degree, so the temperature of the water rises more slowly.
misconceptions.misconception: A substance with a high specific heat capacity heats up quickly, because it has a high 'capacity' for heating.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of 'high capacity' is 'does a lot', so a big number sounds like a big or fast temperature change. The per-degree structure of the quantity is not carried by the word itself.
misconceptions.correction: Read the definition literally: c is the energy needed for each degree of rise, for each kilogram. A big c therefore means a stubborn substance — a lot of energy for a small rise. Rearranging to ∆θ = ∆E ÷ (m c) puts c on the bottom, where its effect is visible.

misconceptions.question: A block cools from 90 °C to 30 °C. Has the energy stored in it changed?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Its temperature has fallen, so the energy in its thermal store has fallen by m c ∆θ, and that energy has been transferred to the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Temperature and thermal energy are separate things, so a falling temperature need not mean the stored energy has changed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Temperature is the quantity students actually measure and energy is invisible, so the two are easily held apart. The equation links them, but only if ∆θ is read as evidence of an energy change.
misconceptions.correction: For a given system a temperature change is exactly the observable sign of a change in the thermal energy store, and ∆E = m c ∆θ gives the size of that change. No temperature change means no ∆E; a temperature change always means one.

misconceptions.question: A 1 kg block of metal is at 30 °C. Does m c × 30 give the energy stored in the block?
misconceptions.correct: No. ∆E = m c ∆θ gives a change in the thermal energy store, not the total energy the block stores.
misconceptions.misconception: Substituting the block's temperature into the equation gives the total thermal energy it contains.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation looks like a formula for a quantity rather than for a change, and the ∆ signs are easily dropped when the symbols are copied down. Students also expect an energy value to be a total, as it is for many other stores.
misconceptions.correction: Both ∆ symbols matter, and they matter together: a change in temperature gives a change in energy. A total would need a zero point for the energy, and the specification never provides one.

misconceptions.question: Can ∆E = m c ∆θ be used for an object that is cooling down?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The specification says the equation gives the energy stored in or released from a system as its temperature changes, so it covers cooling as well as heating.
misconceptions.misconception: The equation only works for heating, because it is about energy being stored.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every worked example met in lessons involves a heater, and 'thermal energy' is spoken of as something gained. Cooling then looks like a different phenomenon needing a different equation.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is symmetric. A fall of 60 °C releases exactly the energy that a rise of 60 °C would store for the same object, and the specification's own wording — 'stored in or released from' — makes that explicit.

misconceptions.question: In the required practical, does all the energy supplied by the immersion heater end up in the metal block?
misconceptions.correct: No. Some energy warms the air, the bench and the heater itself, so the block gains less than the joulemeter records.
misconceptions.misconception: Every joule the heater transfers goes into the block, so the apparatus needs no insulation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The joulemeter reading is a single definite number, and it is easy to treat a measured value as the value that arrived at the destination. Energy transferred to the surroundings leaves no visible trace.
misconceptions.correction: The measured energy is the energy supplied, not the energy that arrived. Insulating the block and starting close to room temperature reduce the difference but never remove it, which is why the practical has to be evaluated as well as performed.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
misconceptions.correct: Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C.
misconceptions.misconception: The unit is J/°C, because specific heat capacity is the energy needed for each degree of temperature rise.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember the 'per degree Celsius' half of the definition, which is the part repeated most often in class, while the 'per kilogram' half is carried only by the word 'specific'.
misconceptions.correction: Build the unit straight from the definition: energy (J), for one kilogram (/kg), for one degree Celsius (°C). Both 'per' phrases are in the definition, so both must appear in the unit.

misconceptions.question: Must temperatures be converted to kelvin before ∆E = m c ∆θ is used?
misconceptions.correct: No. The specification gives ∆θ in degrees Celsius, °C, and c in J/kg °C.
misconceptions.misconception: Temperatures always have to be changed into kelvin in physics equations, so 18 °C becomes 291 K first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Kelvin conversion is drilled hard in the particle model and gas content, so it becomes a reflex applied to every temperature that appears in any equation.
misconceptions.correction: Check the unit of c: it is per degree Celsius, so ∆θ must be in degrees Celsius to match. A change of one degree Celsius happens to be the same size as a change of one kelvin, but the units the specification states here are °C.

misconceptions.question: Which temperature readings are needed in the required practical?
misconceptions.correct: Both of them — the temperature before heating and the temperature at the end — because the equation needs the temperature rise.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the final temperature has to be recorded, since that is the temperature the block reaches.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The starting temperature is often just room temperature, so it feels like background information rather than data, while the final reading is taken at the dramatic end of the experiment.
misconceptions.correction: The equation contains ∆θ, so a subtraction is unavoidable and both readings are data. Record the starting temperature before switching the heater on, and keep reading for a short time afterwards, as the block goes on warming briefly.

misconceptions.question: How is ∆E = m c ∆θ rearranged to make c the subject?
misconceptions.correct: c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ). Both m and ∆θ move to the bottom.
misconceptions.misconception: Only one of the quantities needs dividing, giving c = ∆E ÷ m × ∆θ.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students move the symbol nearest the equals sign and stop, and read left to right the expression ∆E ÷ m × ∆θ still looks as though ∆θ has been dealt with. Missing brackets hide the error.
misconceptions.correction: Anything multiplying c on one side divides the other side, and here two quantities multiply c. Write the bracket in — c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) — and check the units: J ÷ (kg × °C) is J/kg °C, which is the unit of c.

misconceptions.question: A student rearranges ∆E = m c ∆θ and writes c = (m × ∆θ) ÷ ∆E. What has gone wrong?
misconceptions.correct: The expression has been turned upside down; the correct rearrangement is c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).
misconceptions.misconception: When a quantity is made the subject, whatever shared its side of the equation goes on top of the fraction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is often done by pattern-matching remembered triangles rather than by doing the same operation to both sides, and the reciprocal looks equally tidy on the page.
misconceptions.correction: Divide both sides by m ∆θ and see what survives: ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ) = c. A unit check catches the slip at once, because kg °C/J is not the unit of specific heat capacity.

misconceptions.question: An uninsulated block transfers energy to the room. Is the calculated specific heat capacity too high or too low?
misconceptions.correct: Too high, because the recorded temperature rise is smaller than the measured energy supply should have produced, and ∆θ is on the bottom of c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).
misconceptions.misconception: Losing energy must make the answer too small, because energy has been lost from the experiment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Energy lost' and 'value too low' feel like the same idea, so students judge the direction of the error from the word rather than from where the affected quantity sits in the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Ask which measured quantity the transfer actually changes. The joulemeter reading is unaffected, but the temperature rise is reduced, and dividing by a smaller ∆θ makes c come out larger.

misconceptions.question: A student records the mass, the temperature rise and the power marked on the immersion heater. Can the specific heat capacity be found?
misconceptions.correct: No. Power is energy per second, so the heating time must be measured as well: ∆E = power × time.
misconceptions.misconception: The power of the heater is the energy it has supplied, so no timing is needed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The power is printed on the heater as a single definite number, and both power and energy are spoken of loosely as 'how much the heater gives out'. In lessons a joulemeter often replaces the calculation, so the time never has to be used explicitly.
misconceptions.correction: Check the units: a 50 W heater supplies 50 J each second, so the joules depend on how long it runs. Either read the energy directly from a joulemeter, or measure the time and use energy = power × time before substituting into c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).

mcqs.stem: Which statement gives the specification's definition of the specific heat capacity of a substance?

options.text: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of the whole sample by one degree Celsius.
options.rationale: A student who has not registered what 'specific' means defines the quantity for the sample in front of them rather than per kilogram.

options.text: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
options.rationale: The specification's definition: the energy required, for one kilogram of the substance, for a rise of one degree Celsius.

options.text: The thermal energy stored by one kilogram of the substance at a temperature of one degree Celsius.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat thermal energy as a total held at a temperature, rather than as a change linked to a temperature rise.

options.text: The rise in temperature produced when one kilogram of the substance is supplied with one joule.
options.rationale: This inverts the definition. It describes 1 ÷ c, and it matches the belief that a large value means the substance warms up readily.

mcqs.stem: Which word equation does the specification give for the energy change when a system's temperature changes?

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
options.rationale: The specification's wording exactly: all three quantities are multiplied together.

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity ÷ change in temperature
options.rationale: Students who half-remember the rearranged form c = ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ) sometimes carry a division back into the original equation.

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × final temperature
options.rationale: Uses the temperature reached instead of the temperature change, the commonest substitution error in this topic.

options.text: change in thermal energy = specific heat capacity × temperature change
options.rationale: Leaves out the mass, which appeals to students who think the size of the sample is already accounted for inside c.

mcqs.stem: A beaker holds 300 g of water at 80 °C. The water is heated until it reaches 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the change in thermal energy of the water?

options.rationale: The mass has been left in grams: 300 × 4200 × 20. The answer is a thousand times too large.
Uses the final temperature, 100 °C, in place of the temperature change of 20 °C.
0.300 × 4200 only: the temperature change has been dropped from the calculation altogether.
0.300 kg × 4200 J/kg °C × 20 °C = 25 200 J, with the mass converted to kilograms and ∆θ found by subtraction.

mcqs.stem: Water is heated from 18 °C to 78 °C. Which value should be used for ∆θ in ∆E = m c ∆θ, and why?

options.text: 78 °C, because ∆θ is the temperature that the water reaches.
options.rationale: The final reading is the one the thermometer shows at the end, so it feels like the temperature of the experiment.

options.text: 351 K, because temperatures must be converted into kelvin first.
options.rationale: Kelvin conversion is drilled elsewhere in the course and is applied here by reflex, although c is given per degree Celsius.

options.text: 60 °C, because ∆θ means the change in the temperature.
options.rationale: ∆ means 'change in', so ∆θ = 78 − 18 = 60 °C, in degrees Celsius as the specification states.

options.text: 18 °C, because ∆θ is the temperature the water starts at.
options.rationale: Picks one of the two quoted readings instead of subtracting, the same failure to treat both readings as data.

mcqs.stem: A 250 g metal block is heated by an immersion heater. The joulemeter shows that 10 000 J has been transferred and the block's temperature rises by 20 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J/kg °C?

options.rationale: 10 000 ÷ 0.25 only: the mass has been divided out but the temperature rise has been forgotten.
10 000 ÷ 20 only: the temperature rise has been divided out but the mass has been left where it was.
The mass has been left in grams, 10 000 ÷ (250 × 20), giving a value a thousand times too small.
c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) = 10 000 ÷ (0.25 × 20) = 2000 J/kg °C, with the mass converted to kilograms.

mcqs.stem: Which line gives the units the specification uses for the quantities in ∆E = m c ∆θ?

options.text: ∆E in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, ∆θ in °C
options.rationale: Exactly the units the specification lists: joules, kilograms, joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, and degrees Celsius.

options.text: ∆E in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, ∆θ in kelvin
options.rationale: Right except for the temperature change, which the specification gives in degrees Celsius to match the unit of c.

options.text: ∆E in J, m in kg, c in J per °C, ∆θ in °C
options.rationale: Drops the 'per kilogram' from the unit of c, keeping only the half of the definition students repeat most often.

options.text: ∆E in J, m in g, c in J/g °C, ∆θ in °C
options.rationale: Keeps the laboratory balance's reading in grams and adjusts the unit of c to suit, which the specification does not do.

mcqs.stem: A hot metal block of mass m cools from 90 °C to 30 °C in still air. What does ∆E = m c ∆θ tell you about the block?

options.text: Nothing at all, because the equation applies only while a system is being heated up.
options.rationale: Nearly every worked example involves a heater, so cooling looks like a different situation needing a different equation.

options.text: Its temperature has fallen, but the energy stored in the block has not changed at all.
options.rationale: Holds temperature and thermal energy apart, treating a fall in temperature as no evidence of an energy change.

options.text: The block's thermal energy store has fallen by m × c × 60, and that energy is released.
options.rationale: The specification's equation covers energy released as well as stored, and here ∆θ is 90 − 30 = 60 °C.

options.text: The block is now storing a total thermal energy of exactly m × c × 30 joules.
options.rationale: Reads the equation as a formula for the total energy in the store and substitutes the final temperature.

mcqs.stem: Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C and aluminium has 900 J/kg °C. What does this tell you?

options.text: Water heats up faster than aluminium does when both are supplied with the same energy.
options.rationale: Reads a large 'capacity' as a fast response, when a large c means more energy is needed for each degree.

options.text: Warming 1 kg of water by 1 °C needs more energy than warming 1 kg of aluminium.
options.rationale: The definition applied directly: 4200 J per kilogram per degree Celsius against 900 J for the aluminium.

options.text: A kilogram of water always contains more thermal energy than a kilogram of aluminium.
options.rationale: Turns a per-degree property into a claim about a total stored energy, which the equation never provides.

options.text: Water can be heated to a higher temperature than aluminium can ever be heated to.
options.rationale: Confuses the energy needed per degree with a limit on temperature, blurring energy and temperature together.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 1, how is the specific heat capacity of the metal block calculated?

options.text: By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.
options.rationale: c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ), which links the decrease of one energy store to the rise in temperature of the block.

options.text: By dividing the energy supplied by the temperature rise of the block only.
options.rationale: Moves only one quantity across the equals sign, leaving the mass out of the division entirely.

options.text: By dividing the final temperature of the block by the energy that was supplied.
options.rationale: Uses the single end-of-experiment reading and inverts the division, so no temperature rise is ever found.

options.text: By multiplying the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.
options.rationale: Keeps every quantity on top, the same slip as writing the rearrangement upside down.

mcqs.stem: A student heats a metal block with an immersion heater but does not insulate it. The energy supplied is measured accurately with a joulemeter. What is the effect on the calculated value of the specific heat capacity?

options.text: There is no effect, because all the energy from the heater goes into the block.
options.rationale: Treats the joulemeter reading as the energy that arrived in the block rather than the energy supplied.

options.text: It is too low, because the block has gained less energy than the heater supplied.
options.rationale: Reasons straight from 'energy lost' to 'value too small', without checking where ∆θ sits in the equation.

options.text: It is too low, because the temperature rise recorded is larger than it really was.
options.rationale: Misidentifies which measurement the energy transfer affects, blaming the thermometer readings instead.

options.text: It is too high, because some energy warms the room and the temperature rise is smaller.
options.rationale: ∆θ is on the bottom of c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ), so a reduced temperature rise makes the calculated c too large.

mcqs.stem: Which set of measurements is needed to determine the specific heat capacity of the block in this practical?

options.text: The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the final temperature.
options.rationale: Records only the end-of-experiment reading, so the temperature rise can never be worked out.

options.text: The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the temperature rise.
options.rationale: These three quantities are exactly what c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) needs, measured using AT 1 and AT 5 skills.

options.text: The mass of the block, the power of the heater, and the temperature rise.
options.rationale: Power is not energy: without the heating time, the energy supplied to the block cannot be found.

options.text: The energy supplied by the heater and the temperature rise of the block.
options.rationale: Omits the mass, which appeals to students who believe the size of the sample is built into c.

mcqs.stem: Two identical 1 kg blocks of the same metal are heated. Block X rises by 10 °C and block Y rises by 30 °C. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Block Y has three times the specific heat capacity of X, because it became three times hotter.
options.rationale: Attaches the difference to c rather than to ∆θ, although c depends only on the substance.

options.text: Both blocks needed the same energy, because they have the same mass and are the same metal.
options.rationale: Ignores ∆θ altogether, as if the energy transferred depended on the object rather than on the change.

options.text: Block Y needed three times as much energy as X, because ∆E is proportional to ∆θ.
options.rationale: With m and c the same for both, ∆E = m c ∆θ makes the energy transferred proportional to the temperature change.

options.text: Block Y now stores three times as much thermal energy in total as block X does.
options.rationale: Converts a statement about changes into one about totals, which the equation does not support.
